text:
The Long Way Home: Apollo 13

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Apollo 13 was meant to be the third lunar landing. By then Americans had grown used to the idea, and the networks barely bothered to broadcast the crew's television transmissions. That indifference lasted about three days.

The commander was Jim Lovell, a veteran of three earlier flights who was making his fourth and final trip into space. Fred Haise, a rookie, would pilot the lunar module. The command module pilot was supposed to be Ken Mattingly, but days before launch doctors learned he had been exposed to German measles. Mattingly had no immunity, so NASA replaced him with the backup, Jack Swigert, who had trained for the job only a few days. The crew called their command ship Odyssey and their lunar lander Aquarius.

The first two days went smoothly. The ship coasted outward, and the crew checked systems and ate meals. Then, on the evening of April 13, about 56 hours into the flight and roughly 200,000 miles from home, Mission Control asked Swigert to stir the oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module. The stirring prevented the supercold contents from stratifying. Swigert flipped the switch.

A few seconds later the crew heard a bang. Lovell felt the spacecraft shudder. Warning lights lit up, and the voltage readings started to fall. Swigert radioed the now-famous words: "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it, a little more precisely: "Houston, we've had a problem."

The cause lay in an oxygen tank that had been damaged years earlier on the ground. During a pre-launch test the tank's heaters ran far hotter than designed and cooked the Teflon insulation on the wiring inside. When Swigert stirred the tank, a spark from the bare wires ignited the oxygen. The tank ruptured, and the blast tore away a panel of the service module and crippled the neighboring tank as well. The ship's two main electricity sources, its fuel cells, ran on oxygen. Within about three hours both were dying. Lovell glanced out a window and saw the gas venting into space, a plume that told him what the instruments had not yet confirmed. "It looks to me, looking out of the hatch, that we are venting something," he reported. "It's a gas of some sort."

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz gathered his controllers. At first they tried to save the command module, but the numbers kept getting worse. Odyssey would run out of power and oxygen long before it could get home. The only lifeboat was the lunar module, Aquarius, which had been built to keep two men alive for about two days on the Moon, not three men for four days in deep space. The crew powered down Odyssey and crowded into the lander.

The next question was which way to go. The spacecraft was on a path that would loop around the Moon and return toward Earth, though not close enough to be safe, and the service module engine could no longer be trusted. Controllers decided to use the lander's descent engine, designed to brake a landing, to speed the trip home. After the ship swung around the far side of the Moon, the crew fired the engine for about four and a half minutes. It put them on a course for splashdown in the Pacific, and it shortened the return by hours. During the passage, Apollo 13 reached the farthest distance from Earth any human beings have ever travelled, about 248,000 miles. Nobody had time to enjoy the record. Lovell, Haise and Swigert saw the lunar surface they had meant to land on pass below the window and went on working.

The journey home turned into a series of improvised survival problems. The first was carbon dioxide. Exhaled breath had to be scrubbed from the cabin air by lithium hydroxide canisters, and Aquarius carried only enough for two people for two days. The command module had plenty of canisters, but they were square and the lander's sockets were round. Engineers on the ground assembled a workaround from the materials the crew had on board: plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, hoses from the spacesuits, and duct tape. They read the instructions up to the crew, who built the adapter themselves. It worked, and the CO2 readings fell.

The second problem was cold. With nearly everything switched off to save power, the cabin temperature dropped toward freezing. Condensation formed on the walls. The crew slept little, if at all. Water was strictly rationed because it was needed to cool the electronics, and Haise developed a fever from a urinary infection. They drank little, ate less, and wore what they had.

The third problem was navigation. With the ship's computers largely off and its guidance system in doubt, the crew sometimes had to steer by hand. In one correction, Lovell used the Earth as a reference to hold the spacecraft's attitude while the engine fired. Another time they aligned the ship by the position of the Sun.

Meanwhile, Ken Mattingly, the man who had been grounded, worked in a simulator on the ground. His assignment was to write a procedure for powering Odyssey back up with the tiny amount of electricity left in its batteries, a task nobody had ever planned for. It had to be done in the right order or the ship would not come back to life for reentry. He and a team of engineers worked through the problem again and again, and the checklist was read up to the crew.

On April 17, as the ship neared Earth, the crew jettisoned the damaged service module. Only then could they see what had happened. A whole side panel was gone, and the equipment beneath it was scorched and hanging. Lovell reported the damage back to Houston and photographs were taken. Then they powered up Odyssey and, last of all, released Aquarius, which burned up in the atmosphere after having saved three lives.

Reentry came with a final stretch of anxiety. Radio contact normally drops out for around three minutes while the ship is wrapped in superheated plasma. This time the silence ran longer, and Mission Control waited, unsure whether the heat shield had survived. Then, at last, Swigert's voice came through the static. Odyssey's three parachutes opened, and the capsule dropped into the Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship Iwo Jima, on the afternoon of April 17 after almost six days in space.

A review board, led by NASA's Edgar Cortright, traced the accident to the damaged tank and the series of small decisions that led to it. NASA redesigned the tanks and the wiring, added a third oxygen tank, and carried an emergency battery. Apollo flights resumed the following year, and the program completed several more lunar landings.

Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, and in the narrowest sense it failed. But in the days afterward it came to be called a "successful failure." Its crew came home because thousands of people on the ground and three exhausted men in a freezing lander refused to treat the problem as unsolvable. Of all the Apollo missions, it may be the one that best showed what the program's people were made of.

(approx. 1,200 words)
